I will stay with the crop pattern that fits Quzhou best: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. In Quzhou County, wheat and maize are the main grain crops, and the local system is still dominated by the winter wheat-summer maize rotation. The county sits in the North China Plain, where most rain comes in summer, so wheat usually needs irrigation while maize can lean more on rainfall. Because I am 70, I would keep the plan simple and familiar rather than spread myself across too many crops. I would not chase cotton or vegetables this year. They need more labor, more field watching, and more management risk than I want.

I will assume I am managing 10 mu myself. I would keep all 10 mu in the wheat-maize rotation. For wheat, I would use an improved variety, not save my own seed, and I would hold nitrogen to a moderate rate instead of pushing it hard, because research from the North China Plain shows many farmers overapply N without getting matching yield. I would irrigate wheat 2 times, mainly around jointing and grain filling if needed, because groundwater is tight in this region. After wheat harvest, I would plant hybrid summer maize right away to catch the heat and summer rains. I would give maize less irrigation than wheat, keep fertilizer moderate, use rotary tillage for fast turnover between crops, return straw if possible, and spray only when pest pressure is real. My aim is stable grain, lower water use, and a plan I can actually manage myself.

Sources used: Quzhou crop structure and climate from MDPI on Quzhou County ([link](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4395/13/9/2362)); Quzhou/North China Plain wheat-maize dominance from Nature/PMC ([link](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44264-026-00145-w), [link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/)); irrigation pattern and groundwater pressure from Agronomy/MDPI and Agricultural Water Management ([link](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4395/14/6/1144), [link](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378377424000611)); moderate N rates from Scientific Reports and wheat N study ([link](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-55913-1), [link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6396033/)). I am inferring the `10 mu` farm size because you did not provide land area.
